subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 52-year-old man complains of shoulder pain and weakness when beginning to raise his arm. Examination shows pain and weakness in the first 15 degrees of abduction, and the empty can test is positive. MRI reveals a tear of a tendon of a muscle that originates in the supraspinous fossa.
question: Which muscle is injured, and by which nerve is it innervated?

options.text: Subscapularis, upper and lower subscapular nerves

explanation_correct: The supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) initiates arm abduction in the first 15 degrees before the deltoid takes over, and it is the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle, especially from trauma or degenerative impingement. It is assessed with the empty/full can test. The suprascapular nerve (C5-C6, from the upper trunk) supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Infraspinatus is also supplied by the suprascapular nerve, not the axillary nerve, and it primarily externally rotates the arm in pitching injuries rather than initiating the first 15 degrees of abduction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Teres minor is innervated by the axillary nerve and adducts and externally rotates the arm; it is not tested by the empty can test.
explanation_incorrect.D: Subscapularis is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves and internally rotates and adducts the arm, not abducts it.
explanation_incorrect.E: The deltoid (axillary nerve) abducts the arm from 15 to 90 degrees, not in the first 15 degrees.

educationalObjective: Supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction and is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle (empty/full can test).

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 28-year-old professional baseball pitcher presents with posterolateral shoulder pain and weakness when attempting to externally rotate his arm during the pitching motion. There is no sensory loss. MRI shows tendinopathy of a muscle in the infraspinous fossa.
question: Which nerve innervates the affected muscle?
explanation_correct: The infraspinatus originates in the infraspinous fossa and externally rotates the arm; it is commonly injured in overhead pitching injuries. Like the supraspinatus, it is innervated by the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6), which arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. Isolated weakness of external rotation with a normal deltoid and no sensory deficit localizes to the infraspinatus and suprascapular nerve.

explanation_incorrect.A: The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor; teres minor also externally rotates, but it originates on the lateral scapula, not the infraspinous fossa.
explanation_incorrect.B: The upper subscapular nerve supplies the subscapularis, which internally rotates the arm, not externally rotates it.
explanation_incorrect.C: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior, which stabilizes the scapula and abducts the arm above horizontal, not external rotation.
explanation_incorrect.E: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the trapezius, which elevates and rotates the scapula above 90 degrees of abduction, not external rotation.

educationalObjective: Infraspinatus externally rotates the arm and, with supraspinatus, is innervated by the suprascapular nerve; it is injured in pitching.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 34-year-old weightlifter has difficulty with external rotation and adduction of the arm. Examination reveals atrophy of a small muscle on the lateral border of the scapula that acts together with the infraspinatus. Sensation over the lateral shoulder is intact.
question: Which nerve supplies this muscle?
explanation_correct: The teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle that adducts and externally rotates the arm. It is one of only two muscles supplied by the axillary nerve, the other being the deltoid, consistent with the mnemonic SItS in which the small t stands for teres minor. The axillary nerve (C5-C6) also supplies the regimental-badge area of lateral shoulder sensation.

explanation_incorrect.B: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, the S and I of SItS, not the teres minor.
explanation_incorrect.C: The lower subscapular nerve supplies the subscapularis and teres major, internal rotators, not the teres minor.
explanation_incorrect.D: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi, which extends, adducts, and internally rotates the arm, not the teres minor.
explanation_incorrect.E: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior, which protracts the scapula and abducts above horizontal, not the teres minor.

educationalObjective: Teres minor (axillary nerve) adducts and externally rotates the arm, the t in SItS.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 45-year-old man with a rotator cuff tear cannot internally rotate his arm or bring it across his body. The involved muscle originates from the subscapular fossa and inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus. It is the only rotator cuff muscle that acts as an internal rotator.
question: Which nerves innervate this muscle?
explanation_correct: The subscapularis is the largest rotator cuff muscle; it internally rotates and adducts the arm and is the only cuff muscle on the anterior scapula (subscapular fossa), inserting on the lesser tubercle. It is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5-C6), which arise from the brachial plexus. Loss of internal rotation with a subscapular fossa and lesser tubercle injury localizes here.

explanation_incorrect.A: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, and the axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor; neither supplies the subscapularis.
explanation_incorrect.B: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor, and the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexors; neither innervates the subscapularis.
explanation_incorrect.D: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior and the thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi; these are not rotator cuff internal rotators of the shoulder joint itself.
explanation_incorrect.E: The suprascapular nerve does not supply the subscapularis; only the upper and lower subscapular nerves do.

educationalObjective: Subscapularis is the internal rotator of the rotator cuff (SItS) and is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A physiology student is analyzing the phases of arm abduction from 0 to 180 degrees. She notes that the supraspinatus initiates the movement and the deltoid carries it through the middle range. Beyond the horizontal, the trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula superiorly to allow the arm to reach overhead.
question: Which pair of nerves innervates the muscles responsible for abduction beyond 90 degrees?
explanation_correct: Arm abduction follows a nerve-and-muscle sequence: 0 to 15 degrees supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve), 15 to 90 degrees deltoid (axillary nerve), and beyond 90 degrees the trapezius (accessory nerve, CN XI) and serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve, C5-C7) rotate the scapula. This is summarized by the mnemonic SALT: Supraspinatus, Axillary, Long thoracic, Trapezius. Therefore abduction beyond 90 degrees depends on the accessory and long thoracic nerves.

explanation_incorrect.A: The axillary nerve acts from 15 to 90 degrees and the suprascapular nerve from 0 to 15 degrees; both act before the above-horizontal phase.
explanation_incorrect.B: The musculocutaneous and radial nerves are not scapular rotators and do not contribute to overhead abduction.
explanation_incorrect.C: The suprascapular and axillary nerves cover the first 90 degrees of abduction, not the above-horizontal phase.
explanation_incorrect.D: The axillary nerve acts from 15 to 90 degrees; only the long thoracic nerve of this pair is involved beyond 90 degrees.

educationalObjective: Above 90 degrees of abduction, the trapezius (accessory nerve) and serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) rotate the scapula, the SALT mnemonic.
